weeks.title: Week ending Aug 2, 2026
weeks.overview:
Your reading this week orbited one big question: is the AI capex boom rational, and who pays when it isn't? You read bottoms-up bulls (a breakeven model showing Google's cloud capex covers its cost of capital 3x over; Jamin Ball's cloud run-rates accelerating across AWS, Azure, and GCP) against a growing bear file: South Korea's memory-stock crash wiping $1.2 trillion, Leopold Aschenbrenner's leveraged AI fund going hat-in-hand after a 439% first half, 'spend now, lease later' data-center financing, hidden RSU compensation costs eroding Meta's real margins, and hyperscaler credit spreads widening under $165B of AI bond supply. The credit plumbing got its own thread — securitisation's embedded leverage, private credit's entanglement with insurance, and MBS convexity — with practitioners like Scott Goodwin noting there's 'too much discourse about AI but not enough about leverage.'

Running underneath it all is the book you're reading: Liaquat Ahamed's '1873', where railroad bonds played the role AI data-center debt plays today — a transformative technology, financed by retail-distributed paper and high-pressure salesmanship, that still produced the worst corporate default wave in American history. Your highlights (Jay Cooke's bond campaign, the dismissed warning about 'handsomely engraved railroad bonds', a third of railway bonds in receivership) read like annotations on this week's news.

Around the edges: Paul Graham on great work and real persistence, a frontier-lab agent intrusion post-mortem that doubles as a warning about autonomous-agent security, the political economy of supply chains and Iran, and craft-versus-automation tensions in coding education and AI-era design aesthetics.

lessons_learned.lesson: Separate the returns math from the financing structure. Google's capex clears its cost of capital 3x over, yet the week's blowups (Korea's leveraged single-stock ETFs, Aschenbrenner's fund) were all financing-structure failures, not unit-economics failures. When you evaluate the AI buildout, ask 'who is levered to this?' before 'is it profitable?'

weeks.title: Week ending Aug 9, 2026
weeks.overview:
Your reading this week split into two dominant currents that kept crossing paths: the AI infrastructure supercycle and the plumbing of sovereign finance. On the AI side, you moved from macro (hyperscaler credit spreads, SoftBank's leveraged bet on OpenAI, Nvidia quietly cutting Rubin Ultra memory specs) down to the research layer (Lilian Weng's harness-engineering survey, Anthropic's discovery of a "global workspace" inside Claude, Ankur Goyal's point about judging agents on behavior rather than output) and back up to strategy (O'Reilly's read on Google's DeepMind shakeup as a deliberate Westinghouse-style diffusion play, reinforced by Jeffrey Ding's book on why diffusion — not invention — wins great-power tech races). The throughline is that the AI story is quietly shifting from "who has the best model" to "who controls the supply chain, the scaffolding, and the distribution," with real financial strain (Datadog's customer pullback, Nvidia's memory shortage, SoftBank's borrowing-against-stake maneuver) showing the capex boom isn't frictionless.

The second thread was sovereign and monetary plumbing under stress: Ethiopia's value recovery instruments, the Brady Plan's lessons for today's Common Framework debt restructurings, the BoJ's carry-trade trap, the US-Japan yen intervention, and the shift of Treasury yield price discovery away from FOMC meeting days. These pieces share a skepticism of institutional machinery — VRIs get gamed, the Common Framework lacks the Brady Plan's political coordination, and central banks are reaching for increasingly unconventional tools (repo facilities, euro sales, staggered lock-ups) because the old playbooks no longer fit. A smaller but sharp third thread ran through geopolitics-as-economics: tungsten as a war-prediction market, Hadrian's Wall as a monument to imperial overreach, and the Iran-Oman Strait of Hormuz toll idea, all treating hard-power questions through a market lens.

Your book highlights this week tracked closely with the money themes: The Almighty Dollar's account of the Joachimsthal silver boom reads like a 16th-century startup case study, and its closing highlight — that Toledo/Spain collapsed *because of* silver abundance, not despite it — is a striking echo of this week's supply-glut argument about hyperscaler bonds and the risk of AI capex oversupply.

book_progress.note: This week's highlights follow the book's origin story at Joachimsthal, the 16th-century Bohemian silver-mining town Greeley reframes in deliberately sardonic startup language — a monetary historian even calls it a 'Silicon Valley' of joint-stock capital, and Greeley narrates its IPO-style hype party as 'always an indicator that the founders have gotten ahead of themselves.' The arc lands on the book's central paradox by page 70: Toledo, and by extension Spain, didn't collapse despite an abundance of silver dollars — it collapsed because of them. (A parallel thread from 1873: The Rothschilds also ran this week, tracing Grant-era hero-worship and gift-showering as the excess that preceded the 1873 crash — the same abundance-precedes-collapse pattern from a different century.)

weeks.title: Week ending Aug 16, 2026
weeks.overview:
Your reading this week circled one dominant obsession: where the money for the AI buildout is actually coming from, and how much of it is invisible until it isn't. The Financial Times ran a near-serialized investigation — Goldman's $1.5tn in aggregate hyperscaler lease commitments (a trillion of it off-balance-sheet under GAAP), Morgan Stanley's $982bn-plus in chip/power purchase commitments, Alphabet's obligations alone jumping from $332bn to $811bn in a single quarter, and then Nvidia stepping in to guarantee ~$100bn of credit so OpenAI can build a $500bn Ohio campus. SpaceX, Cerebras, and a viral Twitter thread correcting the Alphabet 10-Q framing rounded out the picture: capital is flowing at a scale that strains the language normally used to describe corporate balance sheets, and multiple smart observers (Wigglesworth, nodiligence, Gundlach) are independently flagging that the accounting hasn't caught up to the exposure.

A second, closely related thread was AI's technical and reputational frontier — midtraining best practices, a genuinely alarming paper on extracting encrypted reasoning traces from frontier model APIs (recovering real API keys and passwords from public agent trajectories), Zvi's breakdown of the Dwarkesh/Greenblatt conversation on recursive self-improvement and scheming models, and the Zuckerberg-vs-Amodei contrast in how labs market their own risk. Dario's own tweet on regulation this week is the coda to that story. Threaded through both AI clusters was a market-history lesson from Damodaran on the Situational Awareness Fund's collapse — a very direct parable about what happens when high AI conviction meets leverage and concentration, published the same week as the SpaceX and Nvidia mega-financings.

Outside AI, you read a cluster on market structure fragility (Treasury market codependency on hedge fund leverage, Jane Street paying up to stay private, UWM's structurally broken mortgage-origination model) alongside a lighter cluster on culture and craft — the Tony P influencer profile, an Economist meditation on Paw Patrol, Lauren Leek's algorithmic-sameness argument, and two well-observed pieces on design taste (Eugene Wei on chart legends, the DMG-installer survey). Your two book highlights from 'The Almighty Dollar' — colonial wealth built on enslaved labor and a passage on how deflation freezes commerce — sit unexpectedly well next to this week's articles: both are about how monetary and capital systems obscure who bears the risk.

weeks.title: Week ending Aug 23, 2026
weeks.overview:
Your reading this week orbited a single big question from several angles: who actually bears the risk when capital, belief, and status get repackaged into something safer-looking than it is? On the finance side you tracked the AI infrastructure buildout from the ground up and the top down — Fergus Finn's two-part deep dive took you from a CUDA kernel launch all the way into GDDR6X latency numbers, while Sascha Steffen and the token-broker piece from vectoral.com showed the financial plumbing above that hardware: $500bn in Nvidia-adjacent financing routed through SPVs into insurance balance sheets, and a gray market quietly reselling unused API credits. The FT trio on US solvency, Treasury buybacks, and Ryan Avent's 'economy running hot' argument all converge on the same macro worry — debt and AI capex are straining the system even though nobody is changing behavior in response, and the softness in the data may be supply-side, not demand-side.

A second thread ran through questions of classification and belief. The FT and Rupak Ghose both wrestled with whether Jane Street is a prop trading firm or a hedge fund, concluding the label matters less than balance-sheet size and directional risk. Meanwhile Adam Bonica's investigation into Democratic fundraising spam and your highlights from Eric Hoffer's 'The True Believer' rhymed hard: both are studies in how institutions exploit belief and identity rather than persuade with facts — Hoffer's point that propaganda only amplifies latent conviction rather than creating it is a near-perfect gloss on the spam-PAC machine bilking elderly donors.

A third, quieter thread was about AI and the self: Bostrom's 'Deep Utopia' conversation, the Rohit Lamba podcast on AI and alienation, Olivia Moore's cheap AI-influencer stack, and a blunt tweet comparing heavy LLM use to 'microdosing alzheimers' all sit alongside Octopusyarn's essay on escaping status games by accepting you're 'a type of guy.' Read together, the week's throughline is legibility versus reality — financial instruments, political labels, propaganda, and even your own cognition all get repackaged into simpler stories that don't quite match what's underneath.

weeks.title: Week ending Aug 30, 2026
weeks.overview:
Your reading this week clustered hard around one question: what happens when the financing behind the AI boom meets reality? Groundbreaker's subprime-ARM analogy for AI compute contracts set the frame, and it echoed through the FT's piece on Nvidia's opaque $200bn 'balance-sheet-as-a-service' credit exposure, the TAM-wars column on SpaceX's and Anthropic's absurd addressable-market claims, zartbot's deep architectural read on OpenAI's Jalapeño inference chip, and Fed officials (Goolsbee, Schmid) publicly worrying about an economy overheating on AI capex. Asterisk's AI Village report added a second, less-discussed angle on the same boom: multi-agent systems fail in ways that individual model improvements can't fix, which matters more as agentic deployments scale faster than anyone is auditing them.

A second thread ran underneath the AI story: the plumbing of debt and credit itself. American Affairs traced how the debt-equity tax distinction — an accidental WWI-era policy never revisited — still shapes who gets to borrow cheaply versus who has to raise expensive equity. The FT's century-long look at corporate bond spreads argued today's tightness isn't unprecedented once you look past the last 30 years, while Druckenmiller's public break with his protégé Bessent over Treasury buybacks, amplified by Brad Setser pointing to Adam Tooze's Treasury-market essays, kept sovereign debt credibility in frame. Layered on top: institutional trust took a hit via Jared Bernstein's essay on a shoddy, unsigned Census report, and Cloudflare's founder-control fight showed how governance 'independence' is often anything but.

A smaller, quieter thread — Debra Satz on markets' moral limits, Raising Cane's cult-like retail devotion, and a 23-months-without-a-smartphone essay on real versus performed 'slow living' — offered a counterweight to the finance-and-AI density, all circling the same theme of what gets commodified and what shouldn't be.
